title: Paul’s missionary journeys
allSummary: All journeys, c. AD 34–62. Tap a chip to focus on one, or tap any city for what happened there, where to read it, and which letters connect to it. Routes are approximate.

0.name: Damascus road to Antioch
0.sum: Journey 0, from the Damascus road to Antioch, c. AD 34–46 (Acts 9:1–30; 11:25–30; 12:25). Saul sets out from Jerusalem to arrest believers in Damascus and meets the risen Jesus on the way. After Damascus (and a time in Arabia, not drawn) he returns to Jerusalem, is sent via Caesarea to his hometown Tarsus, and is brought to Antioch by Barnabas. He makes a famine-relief visit to Jerusalem and is back in Antioch, ready to be sent out on the first journey.

1.name: First journey
1.sum: First journey, c. AD 46–48 (Acts 13:1–14:28). Paul and Barnabas, with John Mark, sail from Antioch to Cyprus, then plant churches across southern Galatia. They retrace their steps through Lystra, Iconium and Pisidian Antioch (not drawn separately), then sail home from Perga and Attalia.

2.name: Second journey
2.sum: Second journey, c. AD 49–52 (Acts 15:36–18:22). Paul and Silas, joined by Timothy, revisit Galatia, then cross into Europe: Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, Athens and Corinth.

3.name: Third journey
3.sum: Third journey, c. AD 53–57 (Acts 18:23–21:17). Paul strengthens the Galatian churches, spends about three years in Ephesus, then travels through Macedonia and Greece before heading to Jerusalem.

4.name: Voyage to Rome
4.sum: Journey to Rome, c. AD 57–62 (Acts 21:17–28:31). Arrested in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar and travels as a prisoner, through storm and shipwreck, to Rome.

5.name: Churches beyond the journeys
5.sum: Churches Paul wrote to or about, beyond the journeys in Acts (c. AD 50–67). Paul never visited some of these (Colossae, Laodicea), and his work in Crete comes after the events of Acts. They are shown here so every church that received a letter has a place on the map.

0: Near Damascus a light from heaven flashes around Saul. He falls to the ground, hears Jesus ask why he is persecuting him, and is led blind into the city. The exact spot is not known; tradition places it near Kawkab, south-west of Damascus.

Saul is led here blind, is healed and baptized through Ananias, and soon preaches in the synagogues. He goes away to Arabia and returns to Damascus. Later he escapes the city at night in a basket lowered through an opening in the wall.
Paul’s hometown, a leading city of Cilicia. He spends some years here until Barnabas comes to find him and brings him to Antioch.
2: Paul and Silas pass through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.

0: Where it begins: Saul, with authority from the high priest, sets out for Damascus. Years later he returns, and Barnabas introduces him to the apostles. Later still, he and Barnabas bring famine relief to the church here.
2: Before the journey, the Jerusalem Council decides that Gentile believers need not be circumcised. At the journey’s end, Paul goes up to greet the church before returning to Antioch.
3: Paul arrives with gifts for the church, reports on his work among the Gentiles, and meets James and the elders.
4: Seen in the temple, Paul is seized by a mob and rescued by Roman soldiers. He defends himself before the crowd and the Sanhedrin, and the Lord tells him he will testify in Rome.

1: Home base. The church worships and fasts, and the Holy Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul for the work. On return they report how God opened the door of faith to the Gentiles.
2: Paul and Barnabas part ways over John Mark. Paul chooses Silas, and the church commends him to God’s grace.
3: Paul spends some time here, then sets out through Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.
0: Barnabas brings Saul here. For a whole year they teach large crowds, and the disciples are first called Christians in Antioch. They carry famine relief to Jerusalem and return, ready to be sent out.

seleucia.m: Port of Antioch, near Samandağ, Türkiye

1: The missionaries go down to the port and sail for Cyprus.
First stop on Cyprus. Paul and Barnabas proclaim the word in the Jewish synagogues, with John Mark helping them.
The proconsul Sergius Paulus asks to hear the word of God. Elymas the sorcerer opposes them and is struck blind, and the proconsul believes. From here Luke begins to call Saul “Paul.”
John Mark leaves the team and returns to Jerusalem. On the way back, Paul and Barnabas preach the word here before heading to Attalia.
The port where they take ship back to Antioch.

Paul preaches in the synagogue, tracing God’s work from Israel to Jesus. The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathers; some Jews oppose him, and Paul turns to the Gentiles, who rejoice. The word spreads, then the missionaries are driven out. On the return trip they strengthen the disciples and appoint elders.
A great number of Jews and Greeks believe, but the city is divided. When a plot to stone them forms, Paul and Barnabas flee to Lystra and Derbe.

Paul heals a man lame from birth. The crowd calls them Zeus and Hermes, and Paul urges them to turn to the living God. Jews from Antioch and Iconium win the crowd over; Paul is stoned and dragged out as dead, but gets up and goes back into the city.
2: Paul meets the disciple Timothy, well spoken of by the believers, and takes him along. The churches are strengthened as they deliver the Jerusalem decisions.

1: The farthest point of the first journey. Paul and Barnabas preach and make many disciples, then turn back.
2: Paul visits the believers here again on his way to Lystra.
During the night Paul sees a man of Macedonia pleading, “Come over and help us.” The team concludes God has called them to preach the gospel in Europe. (The “we” passages in Acts begin here.)
3: On the first day of the week Paul preaches until midnight. A young man named Eutychus falls from a window and Paul raises him to life.

2: The ship makes a straight run from Troas and stops here overnight.
Paul’s first landing in Europe, the port of Philippi.

Lydia, a seller of purple, opens her heart and her household is baptized. Paul frees a slave girl from a spirit, and he and Silas are beaten and jailed. At midnight, as they sing, an earthquake opens the doors; the jailer and his household believe.
3: Paul sails from here after the Days of Unleavened Bread, on his way to Troas.

2: Paul and Silas pass through on the road to Thessalonica.

For three Sabbaths Paul reasons from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise. Some Jews, many Greeks and several leading women believe, but a mob attacks Jason’s house and the team is sent away at night. Paul later writes 1 and 2 Thessalonians to this church.
The Jews here receive the message eagerly and examine the Scriptures daily to see if it is true. Many believe, until agitators arrive from Thessalonica and Paul is sent off to the coast.

Distressed by the city full of idols, Paul reasons in the marketplace and speaks to the Areopagus, starting from an altar “to an unknown god” and proclaiming the Creator and the resurrection. Some mock; a few believe, including Dionysius and Damaris.

Paul stays a year and a half. He works with Aquila and Priscilla as a tentmaker, Crispus the synagogue leader believes, and the Lord reassures him in a vision. He is brought before the proconsul Gallio, who dismisses the case. He writes to the Thessalonians from here.
3: Paul spends three months in Greece before a plot against him sends him back through Macedonia. Romans is traditionally thought to have been written during this stay.

2: Paul has his hair cut because of a vow, then sails for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila. Phoebe, a servant of the church here, is later commended in Romans.
A short visit. Paul reasons in the synagogue, is asked to stay longer, and promises to return if God wills, leaving Priscilla and Aquila behind.
3: Paul’s longest stay, about three years. Twelve disciples receive the Holy Spirit, Paul teaches daily in the hall of Tyrannus, and extraordinary miracles are done. Believers burn their magic scrolls, and the silversmith Demetrius stirs a riot over the goddess Artemis.
5: Timothy is left at Ephesus to correct false teaching and organise the church. Paul writes 1 Timothy to guide him. Ephesians is also addressed to the believers of this region.

2: Paul lands here on his way up to Jerusalem.
3: Paul stays with Philip the evangelist. The prophet Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt to foretell his arrest; Paul answers that he is ready even to die for the name of Jesus.
4: Paul is held here about two years, answering before the governors Felix and Festus and King Agrippa. When Festus proposes a trial in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar.
0: When Greek-speaking Jews in Jerusalem try to kill Saul, the believers bring him down to Caesarea and send him off to Tarsus.

3: Paul’s companions sail ahead; Paul walks the overland stretch and meets the ship here.
A stop on the island of Lesbos as the ship hops down the coast.

Paul calls the Ephesian elders and gives his farewell charge: shepherd the church, beware of savage wolves, and remember “it is more blessed to give than to receive.” They weep, embrace him and accompany him to the ship.
The ship runs a straight course to Cos on the way to Rhodes.
A stop on the way to Patara.
Paul finds a ship crossing to Phoenicia and boards it.

The ship unloads here, and Paul stays seven days with the disciples. Through the Spirit they urge him not to go to Jerusalem; the whole community, with wives and children, kneels with him on the beach to pray.
Paul greets the believers and stays one day.

4: The centurion Julius treats Paul kindly and lets him visit friends who care for him.
The centurion finds an Alexandrian ship bound for Italy and puts everyone aboard.
Sailing is already dangerous this late in the season. Paul warns that the voyage will bring great loss, but the pilot and owner prefer to sail on. A gale from the northeast soon seizes the ship.

After fourteen days in the storm, an angel assures Paul that all 276 aboard will live. The ship runs aground and all reach shore safely. Paul is bitten by a viper and is unharmed, and he heals Publius’s father and others on the island during three months.
A stop on the way up the Italian coast.
Paul finds believers and stays seven days. The rest of the way to Rome is by land, and brothers from Rome come out to meet him.

Paul lives under guard in his own rented house for two years. He welcomes all who visit, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus “with all boldness and without hindrance.” Acts ends here.
5: Romans is written to the church here before Paul arrives. During his imprisonment, the letters to Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon are traditionally dated to these years, and 2 Timothy to a later imprisonment.

A church in the Lycus valley, founded through Epaphras. Paul had not met the believers face to face. He writes Colossians from prison and sends a personal letter to Philemon, a believer here, about the runaway slave Onesimus.
A neighbouring church of the Lycus valley. Paul asks that Colossians be read here too, and that the Colossians read his letter from Laodicea. The church is later addressed in Revelation.
After the events of Acts, Paul leaves Titus on Crete to put in order what remained and to appoint elders in every town. Titus is the letter written to guide that work.
